sources.title: Eight years ago the idea of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel had me captivated, but can Bethesda recapture the magic?
sources.text: Eight years ago, I sat at my desk enthralled. Bethesda had just released the first trailer for The Elder Scrolls 6 , a then mysteriously nameless, locationless sequel to one of the biggest games of all time, and I reckoned I'd just found the secrets to both. It was going to be set in the region of Hammerfell, I reckoned . And the city of Sentinel was a crucial factor in reasoning why. Admittedly, I'm maybe a little more horrified at my level of Elder Scrolls obsession than I am chuffed at any apparent clairvoyance. Ultimately it was a bit of a punt, launched off the back of a day's worth of fanatical hyperfocus and exactly the right amount of the old Gamer Network office's weapons-grade filter coffee. "There's not really a lot to go on here", I wrote, sagely, "but, if we had to, we'd plant our flag in Hammerfell as the location of The Elder Scrolls 6 ." Indulge me a bit and let's retread the reasoning. First, three assumptions were required in order to make any kind of guess at all: The Elder Scrolls 6 would not be set in all of Tamriel; not set outside of Tamriel; and would be set somewhere vaguely close in the timeline to the events of Morrowind , Oblivion and Skyrim - so as to make that bit of scrabbly rock and ruined castle, visible in that now infamous first teaser, at least somewhat traceable with contemporary descriptions in the lore. Then came a lot of narrowing down. Not Morrowind, Cyrodiil, Skyrim or the Summerset Isles, I decided, as we'd been to all of those too recently (I'll leave it up to you whether another eight years since Morrowind lets that one still count as remotely "recent", but still). And then not Valenwood, Elsweyr, or Black Marsh, thanks to the topography of the land in the trailer and the type of environment on show. That left High Rock and Hammerfell, the former of which we ruled out because of its relative size - on the small side for a presumably beefy new TES game - and more importantly, the architecture that seemed at odds with the sandy stone just barely visible in the structures of that first teaser. And finally: Sentinel. The city was perfectly positioned - along a coast with the sea to the right, dry mountains in the foreground, warm stone ruins to the left, no visible land beyond. Now, that setting is all but confirmed - "all but" as, technically , nothing's set in stone yet, pardon the pun. All we've since been shown is a sand dune, an Elder Scroll, the name Sentinel, and a brief quote from a Moth Priest to a Hammerfell High Queen. But we can pretty much lock it in. To the Elder Scrolls obsessive who spent that day eight years ago scurrying down endless YouTube rabbit holes and lingering on the dustiest unofficial wiki pages, the thought of a game set there ought to be tantalising. Already, even with that paper thin new teaser, there's enough to start picking at. The new trailer's quote is dated just four years after the events of Skyrim, for instance, with both that territory and Cyrodiil located right next door, making for some lovely opportunities for crossovers and references to wider events. And the quote itself is curious. As our guides team have already speculated , the notion of "A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate" gives off the faintest whiff of a time-forking Dragon Break. That being the timeline-branching, multiple-player-choice-enabling thing that happened at the end of The Elder Scrolls 2: Daggerfall, a game which took place - aha! - in the Iliac Bay between High Rock and Hammerfell. Surely, the same bay we're looking at in that original TES 6 trailer. It keeps going! The "victory" mentioned in that quote could refer to the victory won by the people of Hammerfell against a Thalmor invasion, in a conflict that - ooh! - took place around the same time Skyrim's main story was happening, and just a few years before that quote is dated. Could we get branching timelines? A tying together of the overarching Thalmor plotline that's been simmering away until now? A load of varying endings, as Bethesda experimented with so openly in Starfield ? I'm off again. Fire up the Unofficial Elder Scrolls Pages! There's such magic here, far beyond the apparent mastery Bethesda has over theory-baiting teasers for suckers like me. These games, for instance, also have an uncanny knack for joyful stupidity. There are Oblivion NPC barks out there that landed right as YouTube's golden era hit liftoff, and in turn defined an entire generation's sense of humour. I was once in a Slack channel here called # reeblereeblereeble , which was just myself and two other writers punting Imperial Watch taunts at each other to lighten the mood every couple of weeks, or whenever someone seemed a bit stressed. When I leave a gathering of old school friends I still catch myself bidding them "farewell!" with Wood Elf gusto, and giggling at the thought of being immediately squished into mulch . And none of that is to mention the design itself, which has at times been more or less unparalleled. The clockwork, systemic magic of Morrowind is extraordinary, the first hour alone a lesson - at least as important as good old over-cited Mario 1:1 - in instructional design. Within a walkable radius of the musty little settlement of Seyda Neen Bethesda gave the player every tool necessary for understanding - and subsequently playing with, then outright breaking - its entire world. With Oblivion it brought the role-playing open world to the masses. With Skyrim it expanded what our very concept of the masses means. By all accounts I should, then, be absolutely drooling at the thought of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. But for some reason the excitement is muted. It's been like this since long before this second teaser, frankly, and for much of that time I've put it down to Bethesda itself. Bethesda Game Studios has not been on a good run. stories.title: How Long Is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake?
stories.summary: You may think you know how long The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but things have changed in the remake. Here's how many hours you'll need to spend with your Switch 2 to finish it.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: How Long Is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake?
sources.text: How long is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time? You may well think you know the answer if you’re one of the many millions who hold Link’s first 3D adventure close to their hearts. But the remake is here almost 30 years later, and things have changed a little. So, just how much time should you put aside to finish the Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake, and can you squeeze it in before GTA 6 arrives? We have three different accounts for you to read through, which detail just how many hours it took, and how that time was spent. I’ve spent 45 hours with Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, across two separate save files. Before I get into my time spent, I will point out that Ocarina of Time only supports one save file ! It kind of gives the impression that it supports multiple – when you start a new game, it only warns you that the five autosave points will be overwritten – but manually saving on your new file will overwrite your original file. I almost lost my 100% file this way, but luckily grabbed it from the cloud save. Onto my stats: It took me 21 hours to reach the credits, and nine more (for a total of 30 hours) to 100% Ocarina of Time. That’s every Piece of Heart, Gold Skulltula, Empty Bottle, and so on. I probably could have done it faster than this; I estimate I took five-ish hours just living in the world and absorbing all of its fine details. Pre-existing knowledge of the original is definitely an enormous help. You can rip through some puzzles, quests, and boss fights when you know exactly what to do. Then, I did it again. I started a new game and beat it in roughly 14 hours. This was mostly mainlining it – and it went fast given that I had literally done all of it just days before – but I still took some extra time to smell the roses and do some extra quests. Up next is the three heart challenge: I’ve never tried that before, but Ocarina’s lack of a hero mode makes me want to set my own challenge. For all my thoughts on those 45 hours, you can check out my Ocarina of Time review . If you take out the time I spent hunting for differences compared to the original game and riding Epona about Hyrule Field, it took me about 27 hours to fully complete Ocarina of Time. That's finishing the story and doing every side quest, alongside finding all of the Heart Pieces and Gold Skulltulas. (And spending at least half an hour doing the Horseback Archery minigame because I've always been rubbish at it.) I will openly admit to being a massive Ocarina fan, so I know this game like the back of my hand, which definitely helped in getting through it as quickly as I did. One aspect I loved about the Switch 2 remake was picking out all of the subtle changes the developers have made to the dungeons. Especially the Water Temple, for obvious reasons. Playing a Zelda game over Christmas is a tradition of mine, so I'm looking forward to a second playthrough where I'll relax and enjoy the world more. And by that I mean spend far too much time riding Epona around Lake Hylia. As our resident Zelda guides expert who has been helping readers through dungeons since A Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds, I tend to take my time when going through Hyrule, making sure I’ve documented every last Piece of Heart, Gold Skulltula, and suspicious-looking rock. In searching every inch of Hyrule Field for anything not found in the original game (did you know fairies leave notes now?), my playtime tends to be a bit extended, leaving me at around 27 hours when I achieved 100% completion and beat the game. Granted, even with some of the new changes, it’s fair to say I grew up on these streets, so more often than not I knew exactly where to go and look for secrets. Still, I haven’t spent as much time as I’d like in the Hall of Fallen Foes, and I’m looking forward to replaying some of my favorite boss battles!

sources.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) review
sources.text: I have a friend who first played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time back in the day, when the game was only just released and he was home from university for Christmas. This is objectively the best of all times to play any video game: not Christmas specifically, but dropped out of the regular world and faced with a few weeks filled with nothing pressing to do whatsoever. Years later, though, my friend told me that the magic of the game didn't just come down to the playing of it, but the way that the playing of it unfolded. Here's what he meant. He'd play all day, curtains drawn, family ignored, working through dungeons and pelting across Hyrule Field on Epona. Then in the evening he'd call his girlfriend, who was back with her own family for Christmas. She always wanted to know what he'd got up to that day. And not in East Sussex; she wanted to know what he'd got up to in Hyrule. So as he played he took regular breaks to tell someone else about what he had encountered, and what he had discovered, and what he had yet to overcome. It is my bright delight today to be able to tell you that, around thirty years later, having just revisited the game in Nintendo's new remake, Ocarina of Time is still worth telling people about. It's still an adventure so surprising, so satisfying, so moving that I need to talk about it. Here's the thing, though. Despite the game being a cast-iron masterpiece, this reaction was something of a surprise to me. Or rather, it was a surprise precisely because the game was a cast-iron masterpiece. In truth, a couple of weeks ago I wasn't really aching to head back to Ocarina of Time after all these years. I kind of dreaded having to slog through an echoing, once-great game and summon a thousand words of measured reverence afterwards. Thankfully I had forgotten two things. The first is that I am an idiot, which means that I had failed to realise that any chance to replay a Zelda should be leapt at. And secondly, it turns out that I'd forgotten exactly what kind of masterpiece Ocarina of Time is. And along with that last point - and we'll get to this properly in a bit - I hadn't realised that there's a secret ingredient to this specific remake that has proved absolutely essential to its greatness, and that has nothing at all to do with the code running on the Switch 2 . Let's deal with remake duties here. This is more or less the game that people played back in 1998. The beats of the adventure, with Link travelling between different eras of Hyrule in order to defeat Ganon, remain the same. You still start in Kokiri Forest and you still ride Epona over the fence at Lon Lon Ranch in one of the great heart-racing, skin-prickling moments in all of art. If you're stuck in a dungeon, you can almost always use an existing guide from the N64 game to work your way through it. The game world is still broken up into little chunks that fade out and in as you move between them. And each game still begins with that unskippably evocative intro that has Link and Epona dashing over a misty hill with the moon behind them, Zelda meets Susan Cooper. Changes though? For one thing the whole game's been updated with modern graphics, and has ditched any and all fixed cameras for a modern system of movement on one thumbstick and camera on the other. One example: Hyrule Castle Town, in my memory at least, always had a central camera and you would pivot about its streets as if you were a horse on a circus merry-go-round. Now it's pure Frozen territory, cobbled paths racing off in every direction and you can explore them with the camera rushing behind you. The game's spaces feel less like elaborate machines that you were a mechanical part of, and more like video game spaces. Yes, from the way I've phrased that I now see that something of a trade-off has taken place here. I loved that sense you got in early 3D games that the whole thing was a clever practical trick that was forever almost about to collapse in on itself, but anyway! The new Ocarina is a game you can show kids who weren't alive in 1998 and they will feel at home more quickly. Sometimes the graphical update is really wonderful. The route to Zora's Domain, which I barely remember in the original Ocarina, is now a lovely scramble over cliffs and arcing crags. A bold smattering of 1990s Nickelodeon colours and glossy textures, meanwhile, makes Jabu Jabu's Belly a cross between a pre-millennium rave and a modern soft play. My favourite locations of all, however, are two of the mid-game dungeons. The Water Temple is now a drowned Art Nouveau palace that you could easily imagine Captain Nemo knocking around in. And the Forest Temple, which is my absolute favourite Zelda dungeon of all time, is a parquet-floored murder mansion that's been overtaken by trees. Dark wood-panelled corridors and weird bits of church sticking out of the foliage. It's the kind of place you'd hear a weird crime podcast about. Trade-offs, however. My wife, a huge fan of the original game, would wander in and out as I played, and often felt the game she remembered was a little more characterful in its visuals. The moment you fight Dark Link, for example, has lost a little of its glitchy liminality, although the staging, with an old tree in the middle of a vast smoky room, is still wonderfully strange. Towards the end of the game, with the trip into Gerudo territory, you could also occasionally be forgiven for wondering if you'd stepped into one of a dozen third-person Unreal games in development at the moment. It's pleasant to look at, but it sometimes doesn't look specifically like Zelda anymore. All that, and some strange character models that inevitably I learned to love, don't really matter very much, however. Not least because a handful of clever tweaks elsewhere mean that Ocarina now races along at an astonishing clip. And all this with a careful paring back of intrusions from Navi the fairy and the owl, who were both there in the original game to help move yo

sources.title: The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Has No Master Quest
sources.text: Master Quest Remake Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is out November 5 in the U.S. and already live for millions of Switch 2 owners in New Zealand and other parts of the world. The good news is that the early reviews have been absolutely glowing for Nintendo’s latest exclusive. The bad news is that they’ve also confirmed there’s no much-requested Master Quest mode. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Master QuestÂ was a reworked version of the N64 game that made it much harder. It was released for the GameCube in 2003 in limited quantities around the launch of Wind Waker . Extremely rare but extremely rewarding for hardcore Ocarina of Time fans who knew the original game like the back of their hands, it functioned as a callback to the more difficult Second Quest for the first Zelda on NES. It was part of the Ocarina of Time remaster on 3DS, too . As a result, many were hoping Nintendo would include some version of Master Quest mode in the Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. According to those who have already finished the game, however, there’s no such option here. “It honestly bums me out that the remake doesnât include a sort of Hero Mode, or even better, the Master Quest variant for veteran Heroes of Time to make us sweat a little too,” Scott White and Alex Donaldson wrote for RPGSite . Anna Koselke, in her review for Gamesradar, was similarly disappointed. “There’s no Master Quest version to play through,” she wrote. “So, for the time being, my journey with the Ocarina of Time remake ends. I’m sent back to the menu screen that still lives rent-free in my head, left wishing I could explore more of this take on Nintendo’s gem, or at least enjoy it once more without losing the mark of my previous progress.” Nintendo hasn’t been shy about delivering free content updates for its Switch 2 games. Star Fox recently received new multiplayer content, and Mario Kart 8 Deluxe even received an entire new 8-player split-screen mode on the newer hardware. It’s easy to imagine a Master Quest mode, or at least a new game+ option, being added to Ocarina of Time in the months ahead, even if it’s not clear what would stop that from being included in the base game from the jump. While players can access the original version of Ocarina of Time on Switch Online, the Master Quest add-on remains absent there as well. Maybe it’ll be added to the GameCube’s growing library on Switch 2 at some point. Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips. Sign up for our free newsletter. sources.title: The Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time Remake é versão definitiva de um clássico quase impecável
sources.text: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time é um daqueles raros jogos que carrega um enorme peso em seu nome. Afinal, ele se consolidou há quase 30 anos como um dos melhores jogos já criados e se manteve nesse patamar mesmo com tantas outras obras incríveis que vieram desde então. Embora tenha envelhecido muito bem, ele ainda possui elementos óbvios que se tornaram datados desde sua chegada em 1998 e, em uma época tão propícia para remakes como agora, fazia sentido que os fãs estivessem ansiosos por uma versão nova e modernizada do jogo. O sonho de muitos se tornou realidade quando o remake de Ocarina of Time foi anunciado para o Switch 2 e teve seu lançamento prometido ainda para 2026. Nós tivemos a oportunidade de jogá-lo por completo antecipadamente por cortesia da Nintendo e te contamos nossas impressões na análise a seguir! Acredito que a primeira questão que surge com um projeto desse é: como você faz um remake digno de um jogo considerado intocável e atemporal por tantos? Praticamente qualquer abordagem seria recebida com algum tipo de crítica, ou porque mudaram coisa demais ou porque não mudaram o suficiente. De qualquer forma, esse remake estava fadado a gerar altas expectativas e a Nintendo precisava resolver o que queria de fato com essa versão. Depois de ver muitos vídeos de gameplay do remake, além de ler entrevistas dos desenvolvedores, eu senti que a intenção era fazer algo bem fiel, mas melhorando tudo o que fosse possível. Foi com essa proposta em mente que me aventurei por mais de 35 horas no jogo para fazer essa análise. Minha expectativa era que não encontraria muitas novidades, mas que veria bons aprimoramentos e um visual totalmente renovado. Para ser bem clara desde o início, já vou dizer que foi exatamente isso que encontrei, mas ainda tive algumas surpresas pelo caminho. Há aqui uma clara inspiração em trazer o jogo mais perto da experiência de Breath of the Wild e Tears of the Kingdom, o que faz muito sentido tendo em vista o grande sucesso de ambos os games e pelo fato deles terem trazido muitos fãs novos para a franquia, com uma porção grande que nunca sequer encostou em Ocarina of Time. Isso é perceptível de várias formas, seja pela melhoria dos menus, pelo novo sistema de acesso rápido aos seus itens, pelo botão de pulo, a possibilidade de correr, a câmera manual ou até pelas diversas novas cenas com NPCs. Se isso é o suficiente para te agradar, é outra história. Imagino que quem queria novos inimigos, diferentes padrões de ataques para os chefes ou até mesmo puzzles inéditos possa acabar se decepcionando. A sensação, até pela narração inicial e a adição da linda tapeçaria que vai se desenvolvendo ao longo do jogo, é que estão nos contando uma história antiga que já ouvimos muitas vezes. Como um livrinho de histórias cheios de figuras cartunescas ou algo meio teatral mesmo. Sabendo o quanto Miyamoto gosta de peças de teatro com marionetes, até entendemos melhor o design por trás dos NPCs, que possuem proporções exageradas e até angulares. Isso condiz bem com a abordagem que a Nintendo tomou aqui. Eles sabem que estão nos recontando algo que conhecemos muito bem e não querem necessariamente mudar nada de substancial. A ideia parece ser celebrar Ocarina Of Time, sem tirar nada de sua essência ou alma, mas resolvendo tudo aquilo que não se encaixa mais em 2026. Pode ser uma aposta segura demais para alguns fãs, mas realmente acho que seria difícil de vermos a Nintendo fazendo grandes alterações em um dos seus clássicos mais icônicos. Partindo para o game em si, não dá para negar que o visual do remake foi motivo de choque para muita gente quando ele foi revelado. Muitos até compararam o estilo com aquelas versões de fãs criadas na Unreal Engine, que focam demais no realismo e ficam sem identidade própria. Acho que isso realmente foi só uma impressão inicial, já que não houve uma vez em que eu pensei nisso enquanto estava jogando. A verdade é que esse novo estilo é cheio de personalidade e se encaixa perfeitamente no tom mais teatral que mencionei antes. Com o novo visual, os desenvolvedores também aproveitaram para caprichar muito mais nos cenários à nossa volta. Tudo é refeito do zero com base no que existia no Nintendo 64, então você acaba sentindo um misto entre um senso de descobrimento e familiaridade o tempo todo. Houve muitos pequenos momentos em que eu entrava em um local novo, quase irreconhecível, mas aí um detalhezinho me lembrava de onde estava e me levava de volta para quando eu caminhava por aquele lugar tantos anos antes Outro fator muito legal de se notar é que há muitos detalhes que deixaram o mundo parecendo mais vivo. O rancho Lon Lon agora realmente parece uma fazendinha no meio de Hyrule, sem tela de carregamento ou aquelas paredes altas em volta. Os NPCs de cada região possuem rotinas próprias que você pode acompanhar ao longo do dia. Até os diálogos mudam conforme o período do dia ou após certos eventos ocorrerem no mundo. É claro que com a mudança dos cenários, naturalmente algumas outras coisas também teriam que ser alteradas. Nesse caso, certos colecionáveis, como pedaços de coração e aranhas douradas, foram colocados em lugares diferentes. Isso só aconteceu com alguns deles, então você ainda encontrará a maioria no local de sempre. Felizmente, o mapa te mostra quantos você pegou em cada local e, após zerar o game, ele ainda te ajuda a ver em que regiões podem estar os que faltam ser coletados. Já a trilha sonora funciona de forma parecida com isso. Ela mantém sua base familiar, mas oferece muito mais aos jogadores. Como agora o ciclo de dia e noite é ininterrupto, independente de onde você se encontra, a Nintendo fez questão de mudar a trilha de cada local dependendo do horário. Então se entrar na vila Kakariko durante o dia, ouvirá aquela linda melodia que conhecemos bem, mas à tarde ela começará ficar mais lenta e quase preguiçosa, enquanto à noite ela se torna mais sonolenta ainda. sources.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time was an unstable 20fps on N64, but the remake is a solid 60fps on Switch 2
sources.text: The greatest game of all time gets a major technical upgrade Reviews for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake are here, and its Metacritic score suggests that it's the best game of 2026. Fans will likely spend years picking apart their feelings on the remake's art style and gameplay changes – hi, it's me, I'm fans – but if there's one objective, unassailable improvement in the Switch 2 game over the N64 original, it's the frame rate. Despite it being lauded as the best N64 game ever made and one of the greatest games of all time, it's fair to say that Ocarina of Time does not meet modern standards for performance. Nintendo capped the original game at just 20fps, and as Digital Foundry demonstrates in a video breaking down the remake's technical evolution, it can dip into the 16fps range in larger environments. "Most other N64 games ran far less consistently," Digital Foundry argues, and I've spent enough time playing N64 games with frame rates dipping into single-digit numbers in recent months (hello, Star Wars Episode 1 Racer) to know that's true. But from a modern perspective it's tough to get over the idea that we ever settled for frame rates this bad, especially when a handful of other N64 classics, like Super Mario 64, were running at a much more playable 30fps. The 3DS remaster of Ocarina of Time would bring the frame rate to 30fps, but the Switch 2 version achieves the dream: 60fps. It's a consistent 60fps, too, as Digital Foundry's analysis says it's "very stable" outside of "very tiny loading hiccups." The game supports variable refresh rate displays, but that's "mostly useless" when performance sticks to the target frame rate so well. The remake's success isn't just about the frame rate, either. In our full Ocarina of Time remake review , Anna says it's "pure magic" and succeeds at "blending the charm and whimsy of the original with more digestible gameplay and stunning visuals." The fact that it does so at 60fps is really just a bonus. There's still time to get your Ocarina of Time remake pre-orders in, if you're so inclined. Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week Dustin Bailey joined the GamesRadar team as a Staff Writer in May 2022, and is currently based in Missouri. He's been covering games (with occasional dalliances in the worlds of anime and pro wrestling) since 2015, first as a freelancer, then as a news writer at PCGamesN for nearly five years. His love for games was sparked somewhere between Metal Gear Solid 2 and Knights of the Old Republic, and these days you can usually find him splitting his entertainment time between retro gaming, the latest big action-adventure title, or a long haul in American Truck Simulator. sources.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake sits before Elden Ring and Skyrim as 26th best game, as per Metacritic
sources.text: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake isn't even out officially yet, but critics have it pinned as one of the greatest games of 2026 – and, apparently, all time. Reviews went live earlier today, marking the Ocarina of Time remake as this year's highest-rated game on Metacritic with a score of 96. For reference, the 1998 original has a near-perfect score of 99 on the platform, with the 3DS version falling behind at 94 – not a low number by any means, mind you. Critics across various outlets (a whopping 81 so far, to be precise) praise the new remake as a behemoth. So, where exactly does that leave the Ocarina of Time remake overall? Well, right in front of both Elden Ring and Skyrim , as per Metacritic's list of the best games of all time, in the 26th spot. Just ahead of it is visual novel The House in Fata Morgana and, perhaps unsurprisingly, Mass Effect 2. It's a testament to how well Nintendo has managed to pull this remake off, I suppose – although, again, it still evidently doesn't touch its 90s predecessor. The remake is intended to boast everything that made us fall in love with the OG some 28 years ago while also bringing new features to the table, from sidequests to dungeon tweaks and Breath of the Wild's option to turn off the UI for more immersion (and, for those up to it, more difficulty). Plus, you know, the jump button we've wanted for decades – if I'm not, erm, projecting myself here. I can certainly see why it's already so highly regarded. Fans will get to experience it for themselves tomorrow, come the Ocarina of Time remake's official release. I'm curious to see how the ranking may change by then, if at all. Want to learn more about why we think that Nintendo's revamped gem is one of the best new games to come this year? Check our The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake review . Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week After spending years with her head in various fantastical realms' clouds, Anna studied English Literature and then Medieval History at the University of Edinburgh, going on to specialize in narrative design and video game journalism as a writer. She has written for various publications since her postgraduate studies, including Dexerto, Fanbyte, GameSpot, IGN, PCGamesN, and more. When she's not frantically trying to form words into coherent sentences, she's probably daydreaming about becoming a fairy druid and befriending every animal or she's spending a thousand (more) hours traversing the Underdark in Baldur's Gate 3. If you spot her away from her PC, you'll always find Anna with a fantasy book, a handheld video game console of some sort, and a Tamagotchi or two on hand. sources.title: The Best And Worst Parts Of The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time
sources.text: Nintendo 64 Nintendo Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time The remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time comes out tomorrow (tonight, if you’re a sicko like me staying up for it), and damn, those reviews look great. It’s a historic game, a classic that people rightfully remember and love for its incredible highs and, with hindsight, in spite of some of its weirdest lows. Having played the original recently, back in January, I can confidently say it’s mostly held up, though a remake smoothing out its roughest edges makes a lot of sense in 2026. Ahead of that launch, though, why don’t we take a quick tour back through Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64 and remember both its best and worst moments? Let’s get some perspective on just what’s in store for us tomorrow before it hits: I mean, just look at him go! I hope this looks just as ridiculous in the remake. Yes, Kaepora Gaebora, I did get all that! Why are your options swapped?! Forget the Water Temple, this is the real worst dungeon in Ocarina of Time . Carrying Ruto around while enemies attack, her crying and returning to the start at the slightest gust of wind touching her, and her berating you the entire time…the bit where she totally gives up if she sits in water really drives me nuts. You’re a Zora! Learn to swim, geez! Genuinely one of the most effective mood-setting moments I’ve ever encountered. Holy crap. What do you mean they don’t allow children to have large wallets? What prompted this law? God this room rules. How different it is from the rest of the temple. How eerie its emptiness seems. The way nothing happens until you cross the room. The structure draws your eye, so you check it out, and finding nothing, you turn to leave, only to see a weird movement near the tree at the center. Step forward and realize your shadow is gone. Navi’s incredible lack of any useful information.Â GOD THIS ROOM RULES. I’m not even going to talk about the boots. Whee! She’s so fast compared to my normal running, and I feel so majestic clop-clopping through Hyrule Field! This is the best way to travel! Epona, please, I am begging you to learn to turn a little. Or jump consistently. It’s honestly more efficient to just roll. I hear this was retained in the remake and I’m so happy. My husband told me there were 100 of these and I still don’t believe him. There’s no way. Ugh, I can’t aim! There’s too much going on! He’s moving too much! The floor is bouncing! Where’s my Lens of Truth?! Agh!!! How was I supposed to know not to break all the pots on the bottom floor before the fight started?! Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips. Sign up for our free newsletter. sources.title: PlayStation’s Black Friday Sale Is Live With Big Discounts on Digital PS5 Games
sources.text: It’s official: Black Friday season is upon us. As Sony announced yesterday , the PlayStation Store has kicked off its Black Friday sale (you can see the whole sale here ). This portion of the sale runs November 4 - 20, dropping prices on thousands of digital PS5 games. These range from older titles you’d expect to get discounts to new 2026 games like Wolverine, Control Resonant, Silent Hill: Townfall, and many more. Let’s take a look. Before we dive in, a couple of things to note. First, Sony once again appears to be using dynamic pricing in this sale. When I was signed out, I saw Astro Bot on sale for $39.59. After I signed in (and I don't have PS Plus), it showed me $33.59. So your mileage may vary on the exact prices. Second, these deals are just the beginning of the Black Friday season, and they may not be the best deals we'll see on these games. With Black Friday coming in just a few weeks, other retailers will certainly have some of these games on sale as well, likely for lower prices in some cases. So keep that in mind when planning your purchases. With that out of the way, let’s look at what’s on sale. The biggest first-party PS5 game of the fall is Marvel’s Wolverine, from Insomniac, the makers of the Spider-Man PS5 games. It’s a fun (and very gory) single-player action game that tells a good story, though our reviewer scored it a 6/10 . Only the digital deluxe edition is on sale, but the discount actually makes it cheaper than the standard edition by $10. In addition to get base game, it includes a host of exclusive suits and claw skins, as well as some in-game help in the form of Technique Points. On the other hand, if you have a PS5 with a disc drive, you can get a pre-owned copy of the standard edition on sale at GameStop for $38.99 right now. That's an example of other retailers possibly offering bigger discounts than you'll find in the PlayStation Store's sale. The more flexible you can be in terms of format and retailer, the better deals you'll be able to score this month. As for other games on sale, Control Resonant is another big new game of the fall. And once again, it’s the digital deluxe edition that’s on sale instead of the standard edition. It comes with an extra outfit, a starter resource bundle, and a digital artbook and soundtrack. The deluxe edition of 007: First Light is on sale for 50% off; it also includes some in-game outfits and extras. If standard editions are more your speed and you dig horror, you can pick up Silent Hill: Townfall for a cool 20% off. Beast of Reincarnation is on sale for 25% off. And a whole lot more games are discounted as well. But once again, if you want the best deals possible, you’ll likely find bigger discounts in the weeks to come. If you want my advice, for now just buy the games you’ll start playing very soon. For everything else, make a list of what games you want and keep an eye out for all the PS5 game sales to come. Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's LEGO coverage and maintains the upcoming release dates articles for video games , LEGO sets , and 4K Blu-rays . sources.title: Sonic the Hedgehog is in The Angry Birds Movie 3 for some reason, and people are confused
sources.text: Sonic makes a blink-and-you'll-miss-it appearance in the new Angry Birds 3 trailer If you thought you'd have to wait till next March to see Sonic the Hedgehog at the theater again in Sonic 4 , boy do we have good news: the blue blur will appear in this December's animated sequel Angry Birds 3 for, er, no particular reason we can discern. The surprise appearance is revealed/spoiled in the movie's second official trailer , which features a very brief shot of Sonic running at super-speed alongside yellow canary Chuck (voiced by Josh Gad in the movies). Other than that, there's zero context for why Sonic is suddenly a part of the Angry Birds franchise despite not having appeared in the first two movies. Check it out below. The top comment on YouTube right now sums up the general feeling: "WHAT IS SONIC DOING HERE THIS FEELS LIKE I'M HAVING A FEVER DREAM." The truth is likely that this is just a bit of corporate synergy. Sega bought Angry Birds studio Rovio back in 2023. It stands to reason that they might want to give Angry Birds 3, which is arriving 7 years after the last movie and long after the mobile game's peak, a boost given Sonic's big-screen popularity. We don't yet know if either 'live-action' Sonic Ben Schwartz or animated Sonic voice actor Roger Craig Smith will reprise their Sonic roles for Angry Birds 3. Angry Birds 3 will see Red (Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis) take on his biggest challenge yet: fatherhood, to three little birds who don't even seem all that angry from the trailer. The movie will face stiff competition in theaters, as it's releasing alongside Jumanji 3 , and hot on the heels of Avengers: Doomsday and Dune 3 . The Angry Birds Movie 3 releases in theaters on December 25. For more, check out our ranking of the best video game movies . sources.title: Preview Two New Ways to Play with XBOX Cloud Gaming
sources.text: Starting today, we’re rolling out two previews for XBOX Cloud Gaming. On supported Smart TVs, you can use your phone as a controller when you don’t have one nearby. In the US, you can also preview cloud connect with the new XBOX Nano Controller. It uses Wi-Fi to connect directly to your cloud gaming session, which can help make gameplay feel more responsive. Both experiences are still being tested. Availability and supported games or devices may be limited while we learn from your feedback. Want to play a cloud game on your TV but don’t have a controller handy? In this preview, you can use a supported Android or iOS phone as your controller on a supported Smart TV . The controls open in your phone’s browser, so you don’t need a separate controller. Some games will also have controls tailored to how they play. To try it, turn on Preview Features under Settings > Account in the latest supported Smart TV experience. When you launch a game without a physical controller connected, you’ll see an option to use your phone for that session. The preview is rolling out today on supported TVs, in countries where XBOX Cloud Gaming is supported. Players in the U.S. can preview cloud connect with the XBOX Nano Controller starting today. Instead of a Bluetooth connection to your TV, cloud connect uses your Wi-Fi to connect directly to the cloud server running your game. That can help reduce input latency, so gameplay may feel more responsive. Cloud connect is still an early test, so it won’t work with every cloud gaming experience yet. For now, you can try it on supported Smart TVs and the web. Check out the cloud connect setup guide for detailed instructions: https://support.xbox.com/en-US/help/hardware-network/controller/cloud-connect . We’re testing both experiences to learn what works well and what needs improvement. If you have a suggestion or run into an issue, please share your feedback through the preview experience. We’ll use what we learn to help shape future updates.

sources.title: Xbox previews two new ways to control cloud games
sources.text: Xbox Cloud Gaming is getting a phone controller and new direct Wi-Fi connectivity for the Xbox Nano. Xbox Cloud Gaming is getting a phone controller and new direct Wi-Fi connectivity for the Xbox Nano. I revealed yesterday that the new Xbox Nano controller supports a Wi-Fi connection directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming, and now Microsoft is making it official today. Two new Xbox previews will let players try out using a phone as a controller on smart TVs, as well as cloud connect on the Xbox Nano to connect directly to cloud servers. “Instead of a Bluetooth connection to your TV, cloud connect uses your Wi-Fi to connect directly to the cloud server running your game,” says the Xbox team . “That can help reduce input latency, so gameplay may feel more responsive.” Players in the US will be able to preview the new cloud connect option for the Xbox Nano controller starting today. If you’re not in the US you will be able to preview a new phone controller option on smart TVs. The controller is available on the Xbox Cloud Gaming website, allowing people to use the streaming service without a dedicated Bluetooth controller. Microsoft says “both experiences are still being tested” and that “availability and supported games or devices may be limited” during this beta phase. You’ll need to use the Xbox beta app for Android or the Xbox Accessories app on PC to set up cloud connect on the Nano controller, and the smart TV phone controller just requires a toggle of preview features from the Settings > Account section of Xbox Cloud Gaming.

sources.name: Insider Gaming
sources.title: XBOX Announces Two New Cloud Gaming Options
sources.text: The “This is an XBOX” mantra continues on, this time with two new options reportedly being tested out for the brand’s Cloud Gaming service. Already a robust offering of streaming options, XBOX Cloud Gaming has been compatible with multiple gamepads (including a PS4 DualShock) and with multiple devices, such as phones, tablets, PCs, and more. Now, XBOX seems primed to add a couple more ways to enjoy their Cloud Gaming platform. Revealed today via XBOX Wire , the first of two new XBOX Cloud Gaming options includes simply connecting your compatible smartphone to a supported Smart TV. The list of Smart TV options is, admittedly, not staggering , but still includes many popular models like Amazon Fire, LG, Samsung, and certain VIDAA OS-Powered units. With the correct television, you’re now able to download the XBOX app and toggle on “Preview Features” in your account settings. When launching the app without a controller connected, the XBOX Smart TV app is supposed to then prompt you to use your phone (Android or iOS) as a controller, and away you go. I personally have a compatible Smart TV and phone, yet I was not getting this prompt when testing myself. However, XBOX Wire mentioned this feature is “rolling out” today, so perhaps the update hasn’t reached me yet. Regardless, being able to simply connect and use a smartphone to stream games on TV is a nice lowering of the barrier to entry for XBOX Cloud Gaming. The other new option revealed today for XBOX Cloud Gaming is connecting the new XBOX Nano Controller ($49.99) to your device of choice via the same WiFi network that you are streaming from. In theory, this seems like a great streaming setup, given that the Nano controller is literally pocket-sized. This should mean your options for Cloud Gaming situations are now more extensive than ever. What’s your most likely use case for XBOX Cloud Gaming? Let us know your thoughts at the Insider Gaming Discord server . Looking for more XBOX news? Check out our story on the XBOX Game Pass November Wave 1 Titles . For direct access to even more gaming coverage, make sure to sign up for the Insider Gaming newsletter as well. sources.title: Arkane union accuses Microsoft of "sabotaging" Marvel's Blade with 19-month hiring freeze
sources.text: French union STJV says closing Arkane Lyon "would probably be more expensive than finishing the game" A French union representing workers at Arkane Lyon has accused Microsoft of sabotaging development of Marvel's Blade, claiming a 19-month hiring freeze caused the delays now being used to justify the studio's closure. In a statement published today , the Syndicat des travailleureuses du jeu vidéo (STJV) said work on Blade is "going fine" and that the game is on track to meet Arkane's usual quality. It argued that the freeze had led to delays and extra costs, which Microsoft is now allegedly citing as an economic reason to shut the studio. "Today, as work on Blade is going fine, and the level of quality of the game to be expected is on [par] with what Arkane has accustomed its players, workers have to face the harsh reality: our studio might get closed because, and only because, Microsoft decided to, even if that means sabotaging the game it funded," the union said. STJV added that "Arkane is profitable. Just not profitable enough for Microsoft," and claimed that closing the studio now "would probably be more expensive than finishing the game." The Lyon studio's 217 staff, along with contractors and freelancers, face losing their jobs unless a buyer is found. Last month, Microsoft set a November 13 deadline for a sale , which a Microsoft representative later said had been extended by a month, to December 13. The union is calling for workers to have a say in choosing any buyer, and for a fund to protect staff laid off by a new owner within two years. If the studio does close, it wants a $223,000 (€200,000) redundancy payment per worker and two years of Microsoft-funded redeployment support. Microsoft had not responded to the union's claims at the time of writing. Founded in 1999, Arkane is best known for the Dishonored series and Prey. It became part of Microsoft through its acquisition of ZeniMax in 2021. Xbox closed Arkane's Austin studio in 2024. Earlier today, we reported that Ubisoft is reportedly seeking to acquire Arkane Lyon following an extension of its consultation period with Xbox. Ubisoft is currently undertaking a restructuring of its own , as it continues to organize its studios into six "Creative Houses."

sources.title: Arkane union says Xbox is ‘sabotaging’ Blade development
sources.text: The union representing Arkane workers accuses Xbox of “sabotaging” the development of Blade A French union representing workers at Arkane has accused Xbox of “sabotaging” the development of Marvel’s Blade by putting a 19-month ban on hiring new staff. In a statement, STJV (Syndicat des travailleureuses du jeu vidÃ©o) claimed that work on Blade is “going fine”. It admits that there have been internal delays, but allahes that these delays were “artificially caused” by Microsoft , as Arkane was prevented from hiring new developers for over a year. This comes as Xbox considers closing Arkane entirely, although it was reported yesterday that it is also taking bids from potential buyers, including Ubisoft . The union’s statement reads: “Today, as work on Blade is going fine, and the level of quality of the game to be expected is on [par] with what Arkane has accustomed its players, workers have to face the harsh reality: our studio might get closed because, and only because, Microsoft decided to, even if that means sabotaging the game it funded. “The decision to close Arkane is solely the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimisation,” the post continues. “Arkane is profitable. Just not profitable enough for Microsoft.” The union has outlined a list of demands for Xbox. These include giving Arkane a say in who would potentially acquire the studio, and a higher redundancy payout should Arkane be closed down. Right now, Arkane says that the redundancy being offered by Xbox is “outrageously low.” However, Arkane makes it clear that it would like to remain open and continue development on Blade. It also argues that it is in Xbox’s interest to stick with Arkane: “Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game.” Arkane’s future, and the fate of Blade, remain uncertain. Xbox has not responded to these claims outlined by STJV at the time of publication. Arkane was founded in 1999 and is best known for the Dishonored series and Prey. The studio joined Microsoft when its parent company, ZeniMax, was acquired in 2021. The potential closure comes as part of Xbox’s ongoing “reset”, rolled out by the new CEO, Asha Sharma .

sources.name: PC Gamer
sources.title: French game union accuses Microsoft of 'sabotaging' Blade and then using the fallout to justify closing Arkane
sources.text: The STJV union says Microsoft imposed hiring freezes at Arkane that resulted in delays and additional expenses, which it then cited as reasons for shutting it down. "After freezing hiring for 19 months, which artificially caused delays and additional cost, Microsoft now uses those same delays and additional costs as a reason to close down the studio." France's Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo (STJV) union has accused Microsoft of sabotaging work on Marvel's Blade and then using the inevitable results to justify Arkane's closure. The union said development of Blade "is going fine," and that the game is on par with Arkane's previous body of work, which includes the Dishonored series, Prey, Deathloop, and the sadly overlooked Dark Messiah of Might and Magic. Despite that, "workers have to face the harsh reality: our studio might get closed because, and only because, Microsoft decided to, even if that means sabotaging the game it funded." "Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the union wrote. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist. Because after freezing hiring for 19 months, which artificially caused delays and additional cost, Microsoft now uses those same delays and additional costs as a reason to close down the studio." Closing Arkane would defy "financial logic," the union claimed, as it would likely cost more money than just allowing it to finish Blade—and furthermore, it added, Arkane is profitable—"just not profitable enough for Microsoft." "Microsoft is responsible for the situation Arkane is in today. Microsoft is responsible for the situation the workers are in today," the union said. "So Microsoft has to take full responsibility here and act accordingly." While its "dearest wish" is to see Arkane "live on," STJV said the studio's future has to go beyond just completing Blade. And if that's not feasible and Arkane must close, it falls to Microsoft—"the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down"—to take care of the hundreds of lives it has thrown into turmoil. Given Microsoft's essentially limitless resources, the union believes the company has a moral obligation to go beyond the bare minimum required by law: "We will not allow the lives of Arkane Studios' workers to be destroyed without the company paying a fair price." The union is not aiming low with its demands. First, "to give employees control over the decisions that shape their future" while acquisition negotiations are underway: From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews Should Arkane ultimately be closed, it demands Microsoft "funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation" to ensure employees are properly compensated: Those are big asks, but the union isn't wrong about the resources Microsoft has at its disposal: Microsoft's net income for the first quarter of FY27 was $36.6 billion. Xbox is a small contributor to that total, but it is a part of Microsoft, and that makes it Microsoft's issue to deal with. For now, the fate of Arkane remains unresolved: The studio fell victim to the most recent round of cuts at Xbox , but a recent report indicated that it might yet find a home with a new owner . I've reached out to Xbox for comment on the STJV union's demands and will update if I receive a reply. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill. sources.name: PlayStation Blog
sources.title: ‘90s style sci-fi horror Derelikt launches Nov 13 on PS5
sources.text: Solo dev Philipp Jensen reveals the secrets behind the title, which emulates PSOne-era aesthetic. Back in 1999, gaming was good. Games that were released late in the original PlayStation generation squeezed the last drop of performance out of the hardware, resulting in impressive visuals and all-time classics whose sequels we still play today. Fast forward 26 years and we’re excited to announce that our sci-fi horror game Derelikt will make you feel like your console shed 5 generations when it launches on PlayStation 5 on November 13. Derelikt takes place aboard Von Neumann Outpost, grafted onto an anomalous asteroid discovered in Saturn’s orbit. Things are rough. The work is hard, home is a million miles away, and people are stressed out. Plus, a mysterious drone is driving everyone closer to their breaking point… You arrive as an outside contractor tasked with finding out the fate of Excavation Team Delta, who went missing on the derelict surface. What you discover turns things from bad to worse fast! The halls are dark, the systems are failing, and the survivors that you come across aren’t telling the same story. Nailing that feeling of not being able to trust those around you, while simultaneously coming face to face with truly out-of-this-world horrors, was paramount for us. The Von Neumann Outpost is well stocked with an arsenal of traditional weapons, and as you progress, you might even find a few more outlandish weapon prototypes and even alien weapons at your disposal. There are also over a dozen to interact with in Derelikt, each featuring their own secrets, and agendas. Some are useful, some are dangerous, some are doomed, and some (let’s be real, most) are all three! We wanted to not only create this horrifyingly tense world full of scary moments and fast gunplay, but also make sure to make managing resources, exploration, dialogues and old-school puzzle solving a core part of the tension experience. Derelikt is very much inspired by the PSOne-era of sci-fi horror, and it feels like a full-circle moment to be writing this today. The goal was to make it appear as if we found Derelikt on a CD-R in the dusty, long-abandoned storage unit of a defunct late-90s developer and simply ported it to modern platforms. I’m of the firm opinion that retro doesn’t have to mean crude and primitive, and I set out to create the most faithful homage to 5th generation graphics available on the market. Our game features 100% lovingly hand-painted textures and vertex colour lighting. Affine Texture warping was deliberately implemented and mitigated in the next step by dynamically subdividing the geometry – just like the most high-end games of the era did – and the game also features retro-style full-motion CGI cutscenes. This way, a delicate balance was achieved – Derelikt looks aesthetically pleasing while still conceivably plausible on period hardware. Our team made a conscious effort to implement modern game design while keeping the core feeling and charm of that era of sci-fi horror intact, including an option for players to toggle on or off effects to match their particular taste. Derelikt has been in development in some form since late 2021 and has had a turbulent and exciting development journey. We hope the game is as wild a ride for players as it has been to develop! If you’re a fan of PSOne aesthetics, warping textures, geometry, heavy atmosphere, and a sense of unease, all set in the far reaches of space, then we think that you’ll love Derelikt! We hope that you’ll give it a shot, and you can pre-order the game today for a 10% discount, ahead of release.

sources.title: POPUCOM for PS5 launches November 17
sources.text: The PlayStation 5 version of cooperative puzzle platformer POPUCOM will launch on November 17, publishers GRYPHLINE and Fireshine Games , and developer Hypergryph Network Technology announced. POPUCOM first launched for PC via Steam and Epic Games Store on June 1, 2025, followed by Switch on December 4, 2025. Here is an overview of the game, via GRYPHLINE: POPUCOM is a multiplayer cooperative platform adventure game. As an adventurer, you are summoned to an unknown planet to embark on an exoplanet adventure with your friends. You will face various enemies and use engaging items and techniques to eliminate threats and restore the world to its former glory.

sources.title: Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure: Arcade announced for PS5, Xbox Series, Switch, and PC
sources.text: Art of Play has announced side-scrolling arcade action adventure game Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure: Arcade for PlayStation 5 , Xbox Series , Switch , and PC ( Steam ). A release date was not announced. A crowdfunding campaign is planned. Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page : Join Bill S. Preston Esq. and Ted Theodore Logan in this most excellent action adventure 16-bit arcade game! Bag and challenge famous figures from history in preparation for your report, oh and save the world while you’re at it! Play as Bill or Ted, or team up for some couch cooperative multiplayer in this 15-level side-scrolling arcade action game. You’ll get the chance to meet all of the characters from the original movie as you battle through time to save the future. Find Billy the Kid, Socrates, Napoleon, Beethoven and Ghengis Khan and go head-to-head with them in unique mini-games in order to win them over to help you on your quest. High-octane action, lovingly hand-crafted pixel art, and a killer 80s rock soundtrack bring your favorite time-travelling heroes to the arcade… Take on story mode, to unlock arcade mode, mini games and more. Watch the announcement trailer below. View the first screenshots at the gallery .
